summary.text: For arbitrarily large primes \(p\), the only admissible positive integers at most \(p\) are \(1\) and \(p\), so the function has value \(2\). Taking \(\epsilon=\tfrac12\) and a prime \(p>e^4\) gives \((\log p)^{1/2}>2\), contradicting the claimed eventual lower bound.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=\#\{k\in\mathbb N:1\le k\le n\text{ and every prime factor of }k\text{ divides }n\}.
\]
Equivalently, if \(\operatorname{PF}(r)\) denotes the set of prime factors of \(r\), then
\[
a(n)=\#\{k:1\le k\le n,\ \operatorname{PF}(k)\subseteq \operatorname{PF}(n)\}.
\]
We disprove the assertion
\[
\forall \epsilon>0\ \exists N\in\mathbb N\ \forall n\ge N,
\qquad (\log n)^{1-\epsilon}\le a(n).
\]

The key observation is that the sequence is constant on prime arguments.

**Lemma.** If \(p\) is prime, then \(a(p)=2\).

Indeed, the prime-factor set of \(p\) is the singleton \(\{p\}\). Certainly \(1\) is counted by \(a(p)\), because \(1\) has no prime factors, and \(p\) is counted because its only prime factor is \(p\).

Conversely, suppose that \(k\) is counted by \(a(p)\). Thus
\[
1\le k\le p
\quad\text{and}\quad
\operatorname{PF}(k)\subseteq\{p\}.
\]
There are two cases. If \(k=1\), it is one of the two integers already listed. If \(k\ne1\), then \(k>1\), so \(k\) has a prime divisor \(q\). Since \(q\in\operatorname{PF}(k)\) and \(\operatorname{PF}(k)\subseteq\{p\}\), we must have \(q=p\). Hence \(p\mid k\). Because \(k\ge1\), divisibility gives \(p\le k\), while by assumption \(k\le p\). Therefore \(k=p\). Thus the complete set of integers counted by \(a(p)\) is exactly \(\{1,p\}\). A prime is not equal to \(1\), so these are distinct and consequently \(a(p)=2\), proving the lemma.

Now suppose, for contradiction, that the conjectured assertion holds. Apply it with
\[
\epsilon=\frac12>0.
\]
There would then exist an integer \(N\) such that for every integer \(n\ge N\),
\[
(\log n)^{1/2}\le a(n).
\]

Choose an integer \(m\) with
\[
m>e^4.
\]
Such an integer exists by the Archimedean property. Since primes are unbounded, there is a prime \(p\) satisfying
\[
p\ge \max\{N,m\}.
\]
In particular, \(p\ge N\), so the asserted lower bound applies to \(p\). Also
\[
p\ge m>e^4.
\]
The logarithm is strictly increasing on the positive real numbers, and \(\log(e^4)=4\), so
\[
\log p>4.
\]
Both sides are positive, and taking square roots preserves this strict inequality. Hence
\[
(\log p)^{1/2}>\sqrt4=2.
\]

On the other hand, since \(p\) is prime, the lemma gives \(a(p)=2\). The conjectured bound at \(n=p\) therefore says
\[
(\log p)^{1/2}\le a(p)=2,
\]
which contradicts \((\log p)^{1/2}>2\).

Thus the proposed eventual lower bound fails already for \(\epsilon=\tfrac12\). In fact, arbitrarily large primes satisfy \(a(p)=2\), whereas \((\log p)^{1/2}\) is arbitrarily large along those primes. Therefore it is false that for every \(\epsilon>0\), one has \(a(n)\ge(\log n)^{1-\epsilon}\) for all sufficiently large \(n\).
